title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool in university English as a new language (ENL) instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback over feedback from a human tutor. The authors frame the study around broader concerns about the ethical and practical use of GenAI in education, especially for writing instruction where feedback quality, trust, and efficiency matter.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted over six weeks at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. In Study 1, 48 ENL undergraduates were divided into a human-tutor control group and an experimental group that received GPT-4-generated feedback on weekly writing assignments; writing performance was measured with pre- and posttests scored by independent raters. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both human and AI feedback each week and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

Study 1 found no significant difference in writing gains between students who received AI-generated feedback and those who received human tutor feedback. Study 2 found an approximately even split in preference between human and AI feedback, with students valuing human interaction, immediacy, and speaking practice on one hand, and AI’s clarity, specificity, and availability on the other. The authors conclude that GPT-4 feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing support without harming learning outcomes, but recommend a blended approach that combines AI efficiency with human pedagogical benefits.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a comparison group and repeated measures, plus a separate longitudinal preference survey. It is not randomized and has modest sample sizes, so it falls short of blue-tier rigor but provides reasonably credible evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The measured learning effect was null, with no significant advantage for AI feedback over human tutoring. Student perceptions were mixed rather than strongly favorable, indicating unclear overall impact despite practical promise for workload reduction.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-generated corrective writing feedback for ENL students' weekly academic paragraphs and revisions, compared against human tutor feedback
Using ChatGPT/GPT-4 in a teacher-like prompting setup to provide explanatory, sentence-level guidance on student writing

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48; EG n=23, CG n=25), students receiving GPT-4-generated writing feedback made similar gains to those receiving human tutor feedback over six weeks. Repeated-measures ANOVA found no significant group-by-time interaction (F=3.094, p=0.085, ηp2=0.063) and no significant between-group effect on posttest writing scores (F=0.241, p=0.626, ηp2=0.005).
finding.measure: Pre/post analytic rubric scores for writing (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence; max score 40)

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43; weekly survey responses varied from 32 to 41, average 37.7), ENL students were nearly evenly split in preference between AI-generated and human tutor feedback. Mean ratings slightly favored human tutor feedback across satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference items, but differences were nonsignificant and both feedback sources were rated highly (grand means mostly above 4 on a 5-point scale).
finding.measure: Weekly preference survey items on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, overall preference, and forced-choice feedback preference
